name: Phase One: Assess Readiness
title: Phase One: Assess Readiness
answer: Phase One: Assess Readiness is the first step before a school pilots AI, and it asks whether the people, rules, and supports are in place rather than whether the district has enough devices. It matters because readiness gaps, especially around training, guidance, equity, and home access, can stall a pilot or leave some students behind. The readiness check turns each gap into an action item with a date.

sections.body: Readiness means practical training that helps each group understand AI in their own work, not a general course on how AI works. A counselor needs to understand how an early warning flag is built, and a second grade teacher needs to understand what a reading tool does with a child's voice. Readiness also means finding barriers before they surprise the school, because obstacles often arrive in linked clusters such as missing guidance, limited training, and disagreement about what AI education means. The idea solves the problem of launching a pilot on device counts alone, then discovering that staff, families, or students lack what they need. It also puts equity into the check from the start, so access and digital literacy are not treated as afterthoughts.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a district can use a short readiness worksheet that asks whether it has an approved tool list, a data privacy process, a named owner for AI decisions, staff training, and a plan for students without devices or reliable internet at home. Each gap becomes an action item with a date, and Figure 4.3 shows the questions. For a second grade teacher, readiness includes knowing what a reading tool does with a child's voice, while a counselor needs to know how an early warning flag is built. At the sixth grade level, the text points to a study of nearly 4,500 sixth graders in the Netherlands, where digital literacy mattered more than simply using AI tools in class. Every pilot should carry an equity plan that covers students with disabilities and English learners, whose results should be looked at separately when the pilot ends, and it should ask how many students lack a device or reliable internet at home and what they will do instead.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not give a formal evidence label for this idea, but it cites research. Luckin et al., 2022 describe readiness as practical training that helps each group understand AI in their own work rather than a general course on how AI works. Wang & Cheng, 2021 studied two schools in Hong Kong and found that obstacles came in linked clusters, such as missing guidance, limited training, and disagreement about what AI education even means, and that fixing one barrier often eased several others; the same study found schools waiting for government guidance while government waited for school examples. Wang et al., 2026 studied nearly 4,500 sixth graders in the Netherlands and found that family income affected achievement directly and that classroom AI use did not change that advantage, while digital literacy mattered more. Figure 4.3 shows the readiness questions.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits start with the fact that readiness is not about owning enough devices, and a district that hands out AI tools without teaching students to use them wisely should not expect the tools to close gaps on their own. Barriers can cluster, so fixing one may ease several, but schools can also stall by waiting for government guidance while government waits for school examples. Equity work must be part of every pilot, not an afterthought, and the plan must address students without devices or reliable internet at home, students with disabilities, and English learners. Decisions stay with people: the district still needs an approved tool list, a data privacy process, a named owner for AI decisions, and training for staff. The readiness check does not remove the need for human judgment about what to pilot, how to protect students, and when to stop or adjust.
